lesson_title: Push the Rug: How Mountains Get Made and Broken
hook_text: Push a rug across a floor and you've just built a mountain range. Seriously.
clip_script: Put a rug flat on a smooth floor and push one end toward the other. It rides up into ridges and hollows, running across the direction you pushed. Congratulations — you just made fold mountains. That push is compression, and it happens wherever two plates move toward each other. Every up-bump is an anticline, an arch. Every dip between them is a syncline, a trough. Now here's the twist that gets people in exams. You'd expect the arch to end up as the mountain. Often it's the opposite. Bend a stack of newspaper and the OUTSIDE of the bend cracks. Same with rock: the top of the arch is stretched, so it's full of cracks, and rain and rivers go straight for it. Meanwhile the trough got squashed tight and hard. Give it a few million years and the arch has worn down into a valley while the trough stands up as a ridge. The landscape ends up upside down compared to the structure. And you can see the real thing here — drive from Worcester through the Hex River Valley: mountains left, mountains right, vineyards down the middle, repeating for a hundred kilometres. That's a rug that got pushed a quarter of a billion years ago.
visual_style: A rug on a wooden floor buckling into ridges, dissolving into an aerial sweep over the Hex River Valley's parallel ranges and vineyards.
mood: Playful demonstration turning into landscape awe.
pacing: Hands-on and quick at the rug, slower and wider on the newspaper twist, sweeping at the end.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and read any mountain range as a force, a bend and a break.
